questions.q: Toluene is treated with chromyl chloride in CS₂ and the precipitated complex is hydrolysed. The product is:
questions.explain: The methyl carbon is trapped in the Étard complex, C₆H₅CH(OCrOHCl₂)₂, which is not oxidised further; hydrolysis releases the aldehyde.

questions.q: Which reagent does NOT convert toluene into benzaldehyde?
options: CrO₃ in acetic anhydride, then aqueous acid
Cl₂/hν on the side chain, then H₂O
questions.explain: Acidified dichromate (like hot alkaline KMnO₄) oxidises the side chain all the way to benzoic acid; the other three routes stop at the aldehyde.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Étard reaction from the Gattermann–Koch reaction?
options: Étard oxidises the CH₃ of toluene with CrO₂Cl₂; Gattermann–Koch adds CHO to benzene with CO, HCl and AlCl₃/CuCl
Étard adds CHO to benzene; Gattermann–Koch oxidises toluene
Both use CrO₂Cl₂ but in different solvents
Étard gives benzoic acid, whereas Gattermann–Koch gives benzaldehyde
questions.explain: Both give benzaldehyde, but Étard starts from toluene (oxidation of the methyl group) while Gattermann–Koch starts from benzene (formylation).

questions.q: n-Propylbenzene is subjected to the Étard reaction. The result is:
options: Clean benzaldehyde by loss of two carbons
A mixture with benzyl methyl ketone as the major product
questions.explain: Longer side chains rearrange and give ketone mixtures (benzyl methyl ketone major, with propiophenone and chlorinated products), so the reaction is used almost only for ArCH₃ → ArCHO.
